chapters.title: Chapter 5: Costs, Margins, and Taxes of Hedging in India

lessons.title: How Gains and Losses on Hedging Options Are Taxed

children.text: Here is the fact that surprises every first-time hedger. Your index funds and your Nifty puts sit in completely different parts of your tax return. The funds produce capital gains, taxed at fixed concessional rates. The puts produce business income, taxed at your slab rate. So a hedge that works perfectly in the market can still deliver less protection than the payoff suggests, because the taxman takes a bigger share of the hedge's gain than of the portfolio's loss relief. This lesson explains that asymmetry, the set-off rules that soften it, and the filing obligations that come with any options position.

body.text: Options P&L is business income taxed at your slab rate. Fund and share gains are capital gains taxed at concessional rates. A hedge and the portfolio it protects are never taxed as one position, so always judge protection on an after-tax basis.

Section numbers here are from the Income-tax Act, 2025, which applies from tax year 2026-27, with the corresponding Income-tax Act, 1961 section in brackets on first mention. For earlier years, returns still follow the 1961 numbering. Tax law changes with every Finance Act, and your own position depends on your total income and residential status. Treat this lesson as background, not as tax advice, and consult a chartered accountant.

children.text: Which Head Does Each Thing Fall Under?

markDefs.definition: A transaction settled without actual delivery of the underlying. Exchange-traded derivatives are specifically excluded from this definition, so F&O is treated as an ordinary, non-speculative business.

children.text: Exchange-traded derivatives are carved out of the definition of a
speculative transaction

by section 39 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 43(5) of the Income-tax Act, 1961). That single carve-out is why your Nifty puts are treated as a normal business rather than as speculation, and it shapes everything that follows.

body.title: Name the category
body.textWithBlank: Profit or loss from exchange-traded Nifty options is treated as ___-speculative business income.
body.explanation: Exchange-traded derivatives are excluded from the definition of a speculative transaction, so they are an ordinary business. Intraday equity trading, by contrast, remains speculative and its losses can only be set off against speculative profits.

children.text: The Asymmetry: Why a Hedge Protects Less After Tax

Take the familiar hedge: ₹32,50,000 in Nifty index funds, two lots of the 24,000 put bought at ₹250, and a 20% fall to Nifty 20,000. The put pays ₹5,20,000, and after the ₹32,500 premium the gross gain is ₹4,87,500. But that gain is business income. For an investor in the 30% slab with 4% cess, roughly 31.2% of it goes in tax.

body.caption: The same crash, before and after tax (30% slab plus 4% cess, ignoring surcharge)

cells: −₹6,50,000, no relief until units are sold

body.text: This is the single most overlooked cost in retail hedging. The floor you calculated in Chapter 2 was a pre-tax floor. Once the hedge actually pays, a slab-rate taxpayer keeps only about 69% of the payoff, while the portfolio's loss stays locked up as an unrealised capital loss that gives no relief at all until you sell. Plan your hedge sizes knowing the after-tax floor is materially lower than the pre-tax one.

body.title: The after-tax payoff
body.prompt: A hedger's Nifty puts show a net gain of ₹4,87,500 after premium. They are in the 30% slab and pay 4% cess, an effective 31.2%. How much of the gain do they keep, in rupees? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: Tax = ₹4,87,500 × 31.2% = ₹1,52,100. Net = ₹4,87,500 − ₹1,52,100 = ₹3,35,400. An investor in a lower slab keeps more, which is one reason the same hedge is worth more to some investors than to others.

children.text: When the Hedge Loses: The Set-Off Rules
Most of the time your puts expire worthless, which creates a business loss. The rules for using that loss are more generous than many investors assume, with one large exception.

body.caption: Set-off and carry-forward of a loss on hedging options

cells: Against other business income, same year
Against income under other heads, same year, including capital gains, rent and interest
Allowed for up to 8 tax years, but only against business income
Filing your return by the due date
Speculative losses, such as intraday equity, for contrast
Only against speculative income, carried forward for 4 years

body.text: Read the salary row again, because it decides how much the tax system actually helps you. A salaried professional whose only other income is salary cannot use a hedging loss against it at all. A business owner, a retiree living on interest and capital gains, or an investor booking capital gains in the same year can set the loss off in that year and get real relief. The same hedge therefore has a different after-tax cost for two people in the same slab.

body.title: Whose loss is worth more?
body.question: Two investors each lose ₹32,500 of premium on Nifty puts that expire worthless in the same year. Priya's only income is salary. Ganesh is retired, with interest income and ₹6 lakh of realised long-term capital gains that year. Who can use the loss?
options: Both equally, since business losses set off against any income
Neither, since option losses can only be carried forward
Ganesh, because a business loss can be set off against other heads but not salary
Priya, because salary is taxed at the highest rate
body.explanation: A non-speculative business loss can be set off against income under any head except salary in the same year. Ganesh can set it against his interest income and capital gains. Priya can only carry it forward for up to eight years, and then only against future business income, which she may never have.

children.text: What Hedging Does to Your Filing
One options trade changes your return from a simple salaried filing to a business filing. This is not a reason to avoid hedging, but it is a real administrative cost that belongs in the decision.
A different ITR form.
Business income means the return form for business and profession, not the simple salaried form, with a profit and loss statement and balance sheet section to complete.
Expenses become deductible.
Brokerage, exchange charges, STT on your option trades, and a reasonable share of internet and advisory costs can be claimed against this business income.
Advance tax applies.
If a hedge pays off in a crash, that income arrives in one quarter and advance tax is due on it, under section 404 (208), with interest for shortfalls under sections 424 and 425 (234B and 234C).
Possible tax audit.

Audit requirements under section 63 (44AB) depend on your turnover and on whether you use the presumptive scheme under section 58 (44AD). For a hedger placing a handful of trades a year, turnover is usually small, but the calculation is not intuitive.

body.title: How options turnover is calculated, and why it matters

children.text: Turnover for F&O is not the notional value of your contracts. If it were, two Nifty lots would count as ₹32 lakh of turnover and almost every hedger would face an audit. Under the approach in ICAI's guidance, turnover is based on the absolute value of your profits and losses on each trade, added together, rather than on contract value.

So a hedger who buys two lots for ₹32,500 and sees them expire worthless has a turnover of ₹32,500, not ₹32 lakh. Four such hedges in a year give a turnover of roughly ₹1.3 lakh, far below any audit threshold. The picture changes only if you trade frequently or your hedges produce very large gains.

The exact treatment has been debated and guidance has changed over the years, so confirm the current method with your chartered accountant rather than relying on an old blog post. Your broker's tax profit and loss report is the usual starting point.

body.title: The salaried hedger's tax year
body.scenario: Anil, 47, is a salaried IT director in Pune in the 30% slab. In April he buys two lots of Nifty puts for ₹32,500 to protect ₹32.5 lakh of index funds. They expire worthless in June. In July he buys another two lots for ₹32,500. In September a sharp correction takes the Nifty down 18%, and he sells those puts for ₹4,75,000. He does not redeem any mutual fund units all year. His only other income is salary.
body.prompt: Work out Anil's tax position for the year, and what he should do about it.
body.modelAnswer:
1. His options business income for the year is the June loss plus the September gain: −₹32,500 + (₹4,75,000 − ₹32,500) = ₹4,10,000. Both legs are the same business, so they net off within the year.
2. That ₹4,10,000 is taxed at his slab. At 30% plus 4% cess, roughly ₹1,27,920, leaving him about ₹2,82,080.
3. His funds are down heavily on paper, but he has not sold, so there is no capital loss to report and no relief from it. This is the asymmetry: a taxed gain on the hedge against an untaxed, unrelieved paper loss on the portfolio.
4. The gain arrived in September, so advance tax is due on it in that quarter's instalment. Ignoring it means interest for deferment.
5. He must file the business income return form, with the option trades reported as business income, and can claim brokerage, STT and exchange charges on those trades as expenses.
6. What he should consider: setting aside roughly a third of any hedge payoff for tax as soon as it is realised, and remembering that if his puts had simply expired worthless, the loss could not have been set off against his salary at all.
The lesson: for a salaried hedger, the tax system takes a share of the gains and gives little back on the losses. Factor that into how much protection you buy.

body.title: Keep your hedging tax-ready
steps: Download your broker's tax profit and loss statement for the year, which lists every option trade and the charges paid.
Net your option gains and losses for the year to arrive at the business income or loss figure.
If a hedge pays off, set aside roughly a third of the gain for tax immediately, and check the next advance tax due date.
Check whether you have non-salary income in the same year that a hedging loss could be set off against.
File on time, using the business income return form, so that any loss can be carried forward, and have a chartered accountant review the first year you hedge.

body.label: Income Tax Department e-Filing Portal
body.description: Official portal for return forms, advance tax payment and the current text of the law. Use it to confirm rates and due dates before filing.

cards.definition: The head under which exchange-traded F&O profits and losses fall, taxed at slab rates.
Defines speculative transactions and excludes exchange-traded derivatives from that definition.
Long-term capital gains on listed equity and equity funds: 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year.
Short-term capital gains on listed equity and equity funds: 20%.
Set-off of a loss under one head against income under another, except salary.
Carry forward of business loss for up to eight years, against business income only.
Hedge gains are taxed at slab rates while the portfolio loss they offset stays unrealised and untaxed.

points: Options P&L, including hedges, is non-speculative business income taxed at your slab rate, under section 39 (43(5)).
Equity and equity fund gains are capital gains: 12.5% long term above ₹1.25 lakh under section 198 (112A), and 20% short term under section 196 (111A).
A hedge payoff is taxed while the portfolio loss it offsets stays unrealised, so the after-tax floor is lower than the floor you calculated.
A hedging loss can be set off against any head except salary in the same year, under section 109 (71), and carried forward eight years against business income under section 112 (72).
Hedging moves you to the business income return form, brings advance tax obligations, and makes brokerage, STT and charges deductible.
F&O turnover for audit purposes is based on absolute profits and losses, not contract value, so a few hedges a year rarely trigger an audit.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is neither investment nor tax advice. Rates, thresholds and section numbers change with each Finance Act, and the Income-tax Act, 2025 numbering applies from tax year 2026-27 onwards. Figures are illustrative and ignore surcharge. Consult a chartered accountant about your own filing, and a SEBI-registered investment adviser about your portfolio.
